title: The LORD Weighs the Heart
sum: The second half of the first Solomon collection (10:1–22:16) opens with a cluster of sayings about the LORD (16:1–9). People make plans, but the answer of the tongue comes from the LORD (16:1); a person thinks his ways are clean, but the LORD weighs spirits (16:2). Commit your work to him (16:3). He made everything for its purpose (16:4), hates pride (16:5), and accepts loyal love and faithfulness in place of guilt (16:6). The cluster ends with the heart that maps out its road while the LORD fixes the steps (16:9).

Then comes a cluster on the king (16:10–15): his words carry the weight of an oracle, honest scales belong to the LORD, righteousness steadies a throne, and the king's anger and favor mean death and life. The rest of the chapter returns to mixed sayings: wisdom better than gold (16:16), pride before a crash (16:18), kind words like honey (16:24), the road that seems right (16:25, repeating 14:12), troublemakers and gossips (16:27–30), gray hair (16:31), self-control better than a soldier's strength (16:32), and the lot whose verdict is the LORD's (16:33).
readings: Read as a lesson in humility

The chapter's first and last verses frame everything between them: people plan and cast lots, but the outcome is the LORD's (16:1, 33). Read this way, the chapter is not against planning; it trains the young reader to plan carefully and hold the result loosely, since God weighs motives and decides outcomes.
Read as a manual for courtiers

The king sayings in the center (16:10–15) and the many sayings on speech suggest a reader who would serve at court. A young official needed to know that the king's anger was deadly, that honest speech won favor, and that the LORD stood behind just weights and just rulers. The religious sayings around them set the king himself under God.
Read with the rest of Scripture

Christian readers have set 16:9 beside James 4:13–15 ('If the Lord wills') and 16:33 beside the casting of lots for Matthias (Acts 1:26). Jewish readers have linked 16:6 with the teaching that kindness and Torah atone. In both traditions the chapter became a short catechism on providence.

views.H: The chapter reflects life under a monarchy. The king judged cases (16:10), set standards for weights (16:11), and could kill or spare at a word (16:14–15). Merchants weighed silver on balances with stones carried in a bag (16:11), farmers waited for the spring rains (16:15), and lots were cast from the fold of a robe to settle disputes (16:33). Behind all these the sayings place the LORD.
views.C: Critical scholars note that 15:33–16:9 forms a block of 'LORD' sayings in the middle of the collection, perhaps placed by an editor on purpose. Some see 16:1–22:16 as a distinct sub-collection, with more synonymous parallelism than the contrasting couplets typical of chapters 10–15. The Greek text differs sharply here: it lacks 16:1 and 16:3, places 16:6–8 at the end of its chapter 15 (its 15:27a, 28a, 29a), and opens its chapter 16 with a form of 16:9.
views.W: Egyptian wisdom knew the same themes. Amenemope reminds his pupil that "thou knowest not the plans of God" (Budge's translation). The weighing of the heart on scales before Osiris, shown in Books of the Dead, lies behind the image of the LORD weighing spirits (16:2; 21:2). Royal sayings in Egypt and Mesopotamia likewise praised the just king whose throne was founded on right.
views.J: The Talmud reads 16:6 with 21:21 and 23:23 to teach that acts of kindness and Torah study atone (Berakhot 5a–b). Mishnah Avot 4:1 cites 16:32: 'Who is mighty? The one who subdues his impulse.' Rashi reads many of these sayings as lessons about Torah and the commandments. The Targum's paraphrase is close to the Hebrew throughout.
views.X: Christian readers have taken 16:9 and 16:33 as texts on providence, and 16:18 has become a byword ('Pride goes before a fall'). The Greek of 16:6, read as 'by almsgiving and faith sins are purged', was cited in debates on almsgiving and forgiveness; see the card below. Many have heard in 16:32 Jesus' and Paul's teaching on self-control (Galatians 5:23).

deep.b: For these chapters the writer checked the following witnesses directly: the Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text, AD 1008) with its marginal readings, the Ketiv and Qere, as given in the STEPBible edition; the Old Greek in Codex Vaticanus as printed in Swete's edition, with Swete's notes on Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus; the Aramaic Targum of Proverbs and the commentaries of Rashi, Ralbag, Metzudat David and Malbim in the Sefaria editions; Jerome's Latin Vulgate in the Stuttgart critical edition (the Clementine Vulgate, which differs at 18:22, is cited only as reported); the Instruction of Amenemope and the Instruction of Ani in Budge's 1924 translation; and the Babylonian Talmud passages cited, in the Sefaria English edition. The Greek is quoted from Vaticanus; where only one codex has a reading it is named. The Syriac Peshitta and Rahlfs' Greek edition are cited only as reported. No Dead Sea Scroll text of Proverbs 16–22 is known.

Chapter 16 opens with a set of sayings that look at human planning from God's side. A person sets out his thoughts like troops in a line (16:1), thinks his ways are clean (16:2), maps out his road (16:9), and throws the lot (16:33). Each time the saying adds: but the LORD gives the answer, weighs the spirit, fixes the steps, decides the verdict. The same thought returns in 19:21, 20:24, 21:1 and 21:30–31.

The sayings do not tell the reader to stop planning; elsewhere Proverbs praises counsel and careful thought (15:22; 20:18; 21:5). They set the planner under God. The practical result is the advice of 16:3: roll your work onto the LORD, and your plans will stand. The New Testament makes the same point in James 4:13–15.

The cluster 16:10–15 is the longest run of royal sayings in the book, and others follow (19:12; 20:2, 8, 26, 28; 21:1; 22:11). Together they paint an ideal king: he speaks with an oracle's authority (16:10), keeps honest weights (16:11), hates wickedness (16:12), loves honest speech (16:13), and his anger and favor are death and life (16:14–15). The king is under God: his heart is in the LORD's hand (21:1).

For a young courtier the advice was practical: speak honestly, calm the king's anger, seek his favor by uprightness. For later readers, after Judah's kings were gone, the sayings became a picture of what a righteous ruler should be, and Jews and Christians read them in the light of the messianic king (Isaiah 11:1–5).

echoes: James 4:13–15; Acts 1:26; Galatians 5:23; 1 Corinthians 4:4; Romans 8:28; 1 Peter 5:5; Proverbs 14:12; Proverbs 15:33

settings.what: A cluster of sayings on the LORD's rule over human plans
settings.by: the sages who gathered "the proverbs of Solomon" (10:1)
settings.to: young men of Israel's households and, many think, young officials in training
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think, from sayings that may be older; the book links them to Solomon (1 Kings 4:32)
settings.why: To teach a young person who would plan, trade and judge that the outcome of every plan is in God's hands, so that he would plan honestly and trust the LORD (16:3). Knowing these were teaching sayings explains their certainty: they shape habits of trust, not theories of fate.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book, Jews of the Persian and Greek periods and later the church, read these sayings after Wisdom's speeches in chapters 1–9, and heard them as the core of the fear of the LORD (1:7).
views: Many scholars (for example McKane and Fox) think sayings like these were collected to train young scribes and officials at the court in Jerusalem, as Egyptian instructions were in Egypt; the many sayings about kings in these chapters fit that setting.
Others think most of the two-line sayings began as folk wisdom in farming households and towns, and were written down by scribes only later.
Most critical scholars think the collection reached its final form, with chapters 1–9 in front of it, in the Persian period.

settings.what: Sayings about the king: his judgments, his weights, his anger and his favor
settings.by: sages close to the royal court
settings.to: young men preparing to serve the king as scribes, officials or envoys
settings.when: under the monarchy, when a king sat in judgment in Jerusalem
settings.why: To prepare future officials for life near the throne: to speak honestly, keep honest weights, calm the king's anger and win his favor by uprightness, while knowing that the king himself answers to the LORD.
settings.readers: After the exile, with no king in Jerusalem, readers heard these sayings as a portrait of the righteous ruler, and many read them in the light of the king promised by the prophets.
views: Many scholars think the royal sayings point to a school for officials at the court, like those of Egypt.
Others note that ordinary people also needed to know how to behave before a king or his officers, and that sayings about kings need not come from the court.

settings.what: Mixed sayings: wisdom over gold, pride and humility, kind words, troublemakers, gray hair, self-control and the lot
settings.by: the sages who gathered "the proverbs of Solomon" (10:1)
settings.to: young men at home and in training for public life
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think, from sayings that may be older
settings.why: To set before the young the choices that shape a character: to value wisdom above money, to fear pride, to speak kindly, to keep away from gossips and violent men, and to master their own temper. The sayings close as the chapter opened, with the LORD deciding what people cannot (16:33).
settings.readers: Later readers made 16:18 a byword and read 16:32 as a classic text on self-control, in the Mishnah (Avot 4:1) and in Christian teaching on the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23).
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

traditions.q: 16:6 says guilt is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness; the Greek reads 'by almsgiving and faith sins are purged'. Do human kindness and good works atone for sin?
views: Within grace, yes. Scripture and the Fathers name fasting, prayer and almsgiving as expressions of conversion, and works of charity, 'which covers a multitude of sins', among the means of obtaining forgiveness, always as gifts of God's grace in Christ (Catechism 1434).
Almsgiving and mercy heal the soul and draw God's mercy; John Chrysostom preached almsgiving with prayer and fasting as a path of repentance. They are not payment but a share in God's own mercy.

No. Melanchthon's Apology answered Roman appeals to verses like 1 Peter 4:8 and Daniel 4:27: sins are forgiven freely for Christ's sake through faith, and the works such verses praise are the fruits of that faith (Apology IV).

No. Our best works cannot merit pardon of sin; they are accepted only in Christ (Westminster Confession 16.5). The Hebrew of 16:6 speaks of the loyal love and faithfulness by which God forgives and which he looks for in his people.
Works of mercy are a means of grace and necessary for growth in holiness, but justification is by faith alone, and works cannot atone for sin.

title: Quiet, Quarrels and Friends
sum: The chapter opens with a 'better than' saying: a dry crust in peace beats a feast with fighting (17:1). Much of what follows is about conflict in families and between neighbors: the capable servant who takes over from a disgraceful son (17:2), the LORD who tests hearts as fire tests metal (17:3), mocking the poor (17:5), grandchildren as the crown of the old (17:6), covering a wrong to keep a friendship (17:9), the start of a quarrel like a breach in a dam (17:14), and the friend who loves at all times (17:17).

Other sayings deal with justice and with fools. A bribe works like a magic stone (17:8) and twists justice (17:23); acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent are both abhorrent (17:15, 26). A fool is worse to meet than a bear robbed of her cubs (17:12), money cannot buy him wisdom (17:16), and he is grief to his parents (17:21, 25). The chapter ends with the value of restraint: a cool spirit, and silence that makes even a fool seem wise (17:27–28).
readings: Read as household wisdom

Many sayings here concern the family: servants and sons (17:2), grandchildren and fathers (17:6), a brother born for adversity (17:17), and parents grieved by a foolish child (17:21, 25). The chapter teaches peace at home as the first good (17:1).
Read as a guide to speech and silence

From the gossip and the liar (17:4) through the one who keeps bringing up an offense (17:9) to the cool-spirited man of few words (17:27–28), the chapter returns again and again to the tongue. Its ideal is the restrained speaker, a figure Egyptian wisdom also prized.
Read for justice

The bribe sayings (17:8, 23), the twin condemnations of 17:15, and the warning against fining the innocent (17:26) show that the sages cared about courts as well as homes. Their sayings echo the Law's demand for impartial judges (Exodus 23:6–8; Deuteronomy 16:19).

views.H: Israelite households included servants, who could rise to inherit (17:2; compare Genesis 15:2–3). Meat was eaten mainly at sacrificial feasts (17:1). Bribes were carried in the fold of the robe (17:23), surety was sealed with a handshake (17:18), and gold and silver were refined in clay crucibles and furnaces (17:3).
views.C: Critical scholars notice small clusters linked by catchwords, such as 'fool' in 17:7, 10, 12, 16, 21, 24, 25 and 28. The Greek adds lines at 17:5 and 17:6 ('The faithful man has a whole world of wealth'). The Ketiv and Qere differ at 17:27 ('cool' or 'precious' of spirit); see the variant.
views.W: The cool-spirited man of 17:27 matches the Egyptian ideal of the 'silent man', contrasted in Amenemope with the 'heated man' who is like a tree that withers. Egyptian instructions also warn against quarrels and teach that a quiet meal is better than a rich one with strife (compare 15:16–17; 17:1).
views.J: Rashi reads the fool who pays for wisdom with no heart for it (17:16) as one who wants to study Torah without effort. The Talmud cites 17:5 on mocking the poor, applying it even to the dead (Berakhot 18a), and 17:26 in discussions of punishment (Berakhot 7a).
views.X: Christian readers have long taken the friend of 17:17, who keeps loving at every time, as a picture of Christ, who lays down his life for his friends (John 15:13), and have set 17:9 beside 1 Peter 4:8, where love covers a great many sins. 17:22, "A glad heart does as much good as a cure", is among the most quoted proverbs.

deep.b:
Proverbs has a realistic view of friendship. Wealth attracts many friends and poverty drives them away (14:20; 19:4, 6–7). Gossip splits close friends (16:28; 17:9), and some 'friends' only bring ruin (18:24). But "At every time a friend keeps loving, / and a brother is born for the hard days" (17:17); some friends stay closer than a brother (18:24).

The sayings teach how to keep a friendship: by covering a wrong rather than repeating it (17:9), by honest rebuke (27:5–6), and by not wearing out one's welcome (25:17). The ideal friend of Proverbs is loyal in trouble, which is why Christian readers heard in these sayings the friendship of Jesus with his disciples (John 15:13–15).

echoes: 1 Peter 4:8; John 15:13; James 3:5–6; Matthew 5:9; Romans 12:17; Exodus 23:6–8; Deuteronomy 16:19; Proverbs 15:16–17; Proverbs 27:21

settings.what: Sayings on peace at home, friendship, bribes, fools and restraint in speech
settings.by: the collectors of the Solomon proverbs, whose sayings here move between the household, the town gate and the court
settings.to: young men who would soon head households, testify in the gate and choose their friends
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think; the household setting (17:1, 2, 6) is timeless
settings.why: To prepare a young person for life in a household, a town and a court: to keep peace at home, choose loyal friends, refuse bribes, avoid fools and speak little. Knowing these were teaching sayings for the young explains why they paint fools and quarrels so vividly: they are meant to make bad choices look ugly.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book heard the 'son who is a fool' (17:21, 25) as the opposite of the son who listened to his father in chapters 1–9.
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

title: A Strong Tower
sum: This chapter is above all about words. The fool wants only to air his own opinions (18:2); a person's words can be deep water (18:4); a fool's lips walk him into a fight and his mouth wrecks him (18:6–7); gossip slides down like treats into the belly (18:8). Answering before listening is folly (18:13), the first speaker in a dispute seems right until he is cross-examined (18:17), and death and life are in the power of the tongue (18:21).

Two sayings set side by side compare two kinds of refuge: the LORD's name is a strong tower for the righteous (18:10), while the rich man imagines his wealth is a high wall (18:11). Other sayings speak of pride and humility (18:12), the spirit that bears sickness (18:14), gifts that open doors (18:16), the lot that settles disputes (18:18), the offended brother (18:19), the good gift of a wife (18:22), and friends who ruin and the friend closer than a brother (18:24).
readings: Read as a chapter on the tongue
Nearly half the sayings concern speech, and 18:21 sums them up: the tongue has power over death and life. Read this way, the chapter teaches listening before speaking, honest testimony and restraint.
Read through 18:10–11
The pair of refuges at the center, God's name and a rich man's wealth, can serve as the key. Each saying asks where a person finds safety: in pride, wealth, gifts, friends, or the LORD.
Read as wisdom for the courts

Several sayings fit a lawsuit: partiality to the wicked (18:5), answering before hearing (18:13), the first speaker and his cross-examiner (18:17), and the lot that settles a case (18:18). The town gate, where elders heard cases, is the setting.

views.H: Fortified towns with towers and barred gates were the main refuge in war (18:10–11, 19). Lawsuits were heard by elders at the gate (18:5, 17), and lots sometimes settled what evidence could not (18:18). Gifts to superiors were a normal part of court life (18:16).
views.C: 18:8 is repeated word for word in 26:22, 18:11a echoes 10:15a, and 18:12b repeats 15:33b, signs that the collectors drew on a shared stock of sayings. The Greek has an extra couplet after 18:22, and lacks 18:23–24 and 19:1–2, placing a form of 19:3 straight after 18:22. Several verses (18:1, 18:19, 18:24) are textually difficult.
views.W: Egyptian instructions, like Ptahhotep and Amenemope, put great weight on speech: the man who listens, the silent man, the danger of hasty words. 18:13 has close parallels in Ben Sira (Sirach 11:8), and the Talmud links them (Bava Batra 98b).
views.J: The Talmud reads 18:21 as teaching that slander kills (Arakhin 15b). It reads 18:22, 'The one who finds a wife', together with Ecclesiastes 7:26 to ask whether a man has 'found' or is still 'finding' (Berakhot 8a).
views.X: 18:10 has been taken up in Christian hymns and prayers, and the friend of 18:24 who holds on tighter than a brother is often read as a picture of Christ.

deep.h: Death and life in the tongue
deep.b:
18:21 gathers up the book's teaching on speech: 'Death and life are in the tongue's hand.' Words can heal (12:18; 16:24) or wound (12:18), build trust or split friends (16:28), win a king's favor (16:13; 22:11) or bring ruin on the speaker (18:6–7). Gossip is tasty and sinks deep (18:8). The wise listen first (18:13), speak little (17:27–28), and speak truly (12:19).

The New Testament takes up this teaching in the letter of James, which calls the tongue a small fire that can set a forest ablaze (James 3:1–12), and in Jesus' words that people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36–37).

echoes: James 3:1–12; James 1:19; Matthew 12:36–37; Psalm 61:3; Psalm 18:2; Proverbs 26:22; Proverbs 10:15; Proverbs 15:33; Sirach 11:8

settings.what: Sayings on speech and listening, refuge, lawsuits and friendship
settings.by: the collectors of the Solomon proverbs, gathering sayings above all about the tongue
settings.to: young men who would speak in the town gate, as witnesses, litigants and elders
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think, when elders judged at the town gate
settings.why: To train a young man who would one day speak in the gate, testify, judge, marry and keep friends, to listen before answering, to guard his tongue and to seek refuge in the LORD rather than in wealth. Knowing that the sayings were for the young explains their warnings about hasty speech and pride.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book heard 18:10 alongside the Psalms' 'tower' and 'refuge' language, and 18:22 alongside Wisdom's promise that whoever finds her finds life (8:35).
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

title: Poor and Honest
sum: Poverty runs through this chapter. A poor man with integrity is better than a fool with twisted lips (19:1). Wealth brings friends and poverty drives them off, even brothers (19:4, 6–7). Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, who repays (19:17). A poor man is better than a liar (19:22).

Around these the sayings turn to false witnesses (19:5, 9, 28), the king's anger and favor (19:12), the foolish son and the quarrelsome wife (19:13), the sensible wife as the LORD's gift (19:14), laziness (19:15, 24), discipline of children and its limits (19:18), the hothead (19:19), the LORD's purpose that stands (19:21), and the mocker and the naive (19:25, 29). The only 'my son' of the collection appears in 19:27.
readings: Read for the poor

The chapter is realistic about poverty: the poor lose friends and family (19:4, 7) and must beg (18:23). But it insists that integrity matters more than money (19:1, 22), and that God takes the side of the poor and repays kindness to them (19:17).
Read as family wisdom

Several sayings concern the household: a foolish son and a quarrelsome wife (19:13), a sensible wife from the LORD (19:14), disciplining a son (19:18), and the son who mistreats his parents (19:26). The chapter pictures a home where discipline and honor keep a family together.
Read with Jesus' teaching

Christian readers have heard 19:17 in Jesus' words about the least of his brothers (Matthew 25:40) and about giving to those who cannot repay (Luke 14:12–14), and 19:11 in his teaching on forgiveness.

views.H: In Israel the poor depended on family, neighbors and the gleaning laws (Leviticus 19:9–10). Losing family support was a disaster (19:7). Lending to the poor was commanded without interest (Exodus 22:25). Parents depended on their sons in old age (19:26). Courts relied on witnesses, so a false witness could destroy a life (19:5, 9).
views.C: The Greek lacks 18:23–19:2, including 19:1, and has two extra couplets at 19:7 where the Hebrew has a single, probably damaged line. 19:5 and 19:9 are near twins, as are 19:12 and 20:2, and 19:25 and 21:11. 19:1 returns in 28:6 with 'rich' for 'fool'.
views.W: Egyptian wisdom also praised the honest poor over the dishonest rich; Amenemope says the poor man in the hand of God is better than riches in a storehouse. Ancient Near Eastern law collections set penalties for false witnesses, as the Law does (Deuteronomy 19:16–21).
views.J: Rabbi Yochanan said of 19:17: 'Were it not written in the verse, it would be impossible to say it' (Bava Batra 10a), since the verse makes God the debtor of the giver. The Talmud cites 19:23 on going to bed satisfied (Berakhot 14a; 55b). Rashi reads 19:18's 'do not lift your soul to his death' as a warning against beating a son so hard that it kills him.
views.X: 19:17 has been preached in sermons on almsgiving since the early church, often with Matthew 25:31–46. 19:21 is read as a text on God's sovereignty, and 19:11 as a lesson in patience and forgiveness (Colossians 3:13).

deep.b:
Proverbs speaks about poverty from several angles at once. Some poverty comes from laziness (19:15, 24; 20:13) or love of pleasure (21:17). But much comes from oppression (22:16, 22), and the poor are often abandoned (19:4, 7). Wealth brings friends and security (18:11; 19:4) but can be gained wrongly (20:17, 21; 21:6) and gives no lasting refuge (18:11).

Against this realism the sayings set firm values. Integrity is better than riches (19:1, 22; 28:6); a good name is worth more than silver (22:1); rich and poor have the same maker (22:2). God defends the poor in court (22:22–23), repays kindness to them (19:17), and turns a deaf ear to those who ignore their cry (21:13). The book does not idealize poverty or condemn wealth; it judges both by how they are gained and used.

echoes: Matthew 25:40; Luke 14:12–14; Colossians 3:13; Deuteronomy 19:16–21; Ephesians 6:4; Acts 5:38–39; Proverbs 28:6; Proverbs 21:11; Proverbs 26:15

settings.what: Sayings on poverty and integrity, false witnesses, family life and discipline
settings.by: the collectors of the Solomon proverbs; at 19:27 the father's voice of chapters 1–9 breaks in with "My son"
settings.to: sons of Israelite households, addressed once directly (19:27), and those who would care for the poor among them
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think, from sayings that may be older
settings.why: To teach a young person that honesty matters more than money, that God repays kindness to the poor, and that a home is held together by discipline and respect. Knowing the sayings were for future heads of households explains their attention to sons, wives, parents and servants.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book heard 19:27, 'My son', as the voice of the father of chapters 1–9, briefly breaking into the collection.
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

title: Wine Is a Mocker
sum: The chapter opens with wine and beer as a mocker and a brawler, which make fools of those they lead astray (20:1). Royal sayings follow and recur: the king's dread like a lion's roar (20:2), the king on his judgment throne winnowing evil (20:8), the wise king who threshes the wicked (20:26), and loyal love and faithfulness guarding the throne (20:28).

Between them are sayings on avoiding quarrels (20:3), laziness (20:4, 13), the deep purposes of the heart (20:5), the rarity of a faithful man (20:6), the impossibility of claiming a pure heart (20:9), dishonest weights (20:10, 23), haggling buyers (20:14), surety (20:16), fraud (20:17), gossip (20:19), cursing parents (20:20), hasty inheritance (20:21), revenge left to the LORD (20:22), steps directed by the LORD (20:24), rash vows (20:25), the human breath as the LORD's lamp (20:27), youth and old age (20:29) and punishment that cleanses (20:30).
readings: Read as a warning about drink

The chapter's opening verse names wine and beer as characters, the mocker and the rowdy. Read with 23:29–35 and 31:4–7, it is a warning that drink makes people behave like fools, and a call to self-control.
Read as a portrait of a just ruler

The king sayings (20:2, 8, 26, 28) frame a picture of the ideal king who sees evil, separates it out and rules by loyal love. The honest weights the LORD demands (20:10, 23) apply to kings as well as merchants.
Read as a lesson in humility before God

20:9 asks who can claim a clean heart; 20:24 asks who can understand his own way; 20:27 pictures God searching the inner self. The chapter teaches that people do not fully know themselves, but God does.

views.H: Wine was the common drink of Israel, and beer was the staple of Egypt and Mesopotamia; both were drunk at meals and feasts. Merchants carried weights in a bag (20:10, 23) and haggled in the market (20:14). Fields were plowed after the autumn rains (20:4). Grain was threshed with sledges or wheeled carts and winnowed (20:26). Oil lamps burned all night in houses (20:20, 27).
views.C: The Greek lacks 20:14–19 and puts 20:20–22 after 20:9, so its chapter has a different order. 20:10 and 20:23 are near twins, as are 20:16 and 27:13. The Ketiv and Qere differ at 20:4, 16, 20, 21 and 30. Scholars debate whether the royal sayings come from the court or from later reflection on kingship.
views.W: Egyptian instructions warn against drunkenness: the Instruction of Ani pictures the young drinker fallen on the ground with "no one there to put out his hand" while his drinking companions say, "Away with this drunken beast!" (Budge's translation). Amenemope warns at length against false weights and measures. Mesopotamian kings boasted of setting just weights in their law collections.
views.J: The Talmud gathers sayings on wine around the rebellious son of Deuteronomy 21, and reads Psalm 104:15 to teach that a moderate amount gladdens, but excess makes a person crazy (Sanhedrin 70a). It reads 20:27 as calling the human soul the LORD's lamp (Shabbat 30b; 32a). Rashi reads 20:26's wise king as God, who turned Pharaoh's chariot wheels against him.
views.X: Christian readers have used 20:1 in debates about alcohol; see the card below. 20:9 is often read with 1 John 1:8 and Romans 3:23 as a text on universal sin, and 20:22 with Romans 12:17–21 on leaving vengeance to God. 20:27 has been taken as a classic text on conscience.

deep.h: Wine in Proverbs and the Bible
deep.b:
Proverbs speaks about wine in two ways. It is part of a good life: Wisdom sets out wine at her feast (9:2, 5), a prosperous household has full vats (3:10), and wine comforts the dying and bitter (31:6). But it is dangerous: it is a mocker (20:1), the lover of wine will not be rich (21:17), it bites like a snake (23:29–35), and kings must not crave it (31:4–5).

The rest of the Bible keeps the same balance. Wine gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), Jesus turned water into wine (John 2:1–11), and Paul advised Timothy to take a little (1 Timothy 5:23). Drunkenness is condemned (Isaiah 5:11; Ephesians 5:18), priests on duty, Nazirites and the Rechabites abstained (Leviticus 10:9; Numbers 6:3; Jeremiah 35), and Paul says it is good not to drink if it makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21). Jewish and Christian traditions have weighed these texts differently, some urging moderation and others total abstinence.

echoes: Ephesians 5:18; 1 John 1:8; Romans 3:23; Romans 12:17–21; 1 Corinthians 2:11; Ecclesiastes 5:4–6; Luke 14:31; Matthew 3:12; Proverbs 27:13; Proverbs 23:29–35

settings.what: Sayings on wine, the king, honest weights, surety, revenge and the LORD's searching of the heart
settings.by: the collectors of the Solomon proverbs, including sayings that look at life from near the throne (20:2, 8, 26, 28)
settings.to: young men facing the temptations of drink, quick money and revenge, some of them destined for royal service
settings.when: under the monarchy, many scholars think, when a king still sat in judgment (20:8)
settings.why: To warn young men of the dangers that ruin a promising life, drink, laziness, rash promises, dishonest gain and revenge, and to set them before a king who judges and a God who sees within. Knowing these were warnings to the young explains the vivid pictures: the brawling wine, the grit in the mouth, the lamp going out.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book read 20:1 together with 23:29–35 and 31:4–7, so that the book's teaching on wine came to them as one connected warning.
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

traditions.q: "Wine is a mocker" (20:1): does the saying condemn drinking itself, or only being led astray by drink?
views: Being led astray. Wine is a good gift used in the Eucharist; the virtue of temperance avoids every excess of food, alcohol and tobacco (Catechism 2290).

Being led astray. Calvin taught that God gave wine not only for need but to gladden the heart, and that believers may use such gifts with thanks and moderation (Institutes 3.10.2). Some Reformed churches have also urged abstinence for the sake of others.

The tradition leans to abstinence. Wesley's General Rules forbade drunkenness and the drinking of spirits except in necessity, and the United Methodist Social Principles honor abstinence as a faithful witness to God's love while urging care for those harmed by alcohol.

Divided. The Southern Baptist Convention's 2006 resolution declared total opposition to manufacturing, selling and drinking alcohol; many other Baptists see moderate drinking as a matter of conscience.
Abstinence. The Assemblies of God position paper (2016) urges total abstinence, citing warnings like 20:1 alongside the believer's witness and the body as the Spirit's temple.

title: The King's Heart in the LORD's Hand
sum: The chapter opens with the LORD's rule over the most powerful man in the land: the king's heart is like water in irrigation ditches, which the LORD turns wherever he likes (21:1). The LORD weighs hearts (21:2) and prefers justice to sacrifice (21:3). It closes with the same theme: no wisdom or counsel stands against the LORD, and the horse is made ready for battle but victory is his (21:30–31).

Between these come sayings on pride (21:4, 24), diligence and haste (21:5), wealth gained by lies (21:6), the violence of the wicked (21:7), the quarrelsome wife (21:9, 19), the mocker's punishment (21:11), deafness to the poor (21:13), the secret gift (21:14), the man who wanders into the assembly of the shades (21:16), the lover of pleasure (21:17), the wicked as a ransom for the righteous (21:18), the wise man's stores (21:20), seeking righteousness and loyal love (21:21), wisdom that takes a city (21:22), the guarded tongue (21:23), the lazy one's craving (21:25–26), the wicked man's sacrifice (21:27) and the false witness (21:28).
readings: Read as a frame on God's sovereignty

The chapter begins and ends with the LORD's control: of the king's heart (21:1), of the hearts he weighs (21:2), of all human counsel (21:30) and of battle (21:31). Everything in between happens under that rule.
Read for worship and ethics

21:3 and 21:27 frame a question about religion: the LORD prefers justice to sacrifice, and finds the wicked man's offering abhorrent. Like the prophets, the sages insist that worship is acceptable only from people who do justice.
Read as wisdom about home and money
Many sayings concern practical life: the quarrelsome wife (21:9, 19), diligence (21:5), saving and spending (21:17, 20), and generosity (21:26). The chapter's practical counsel rests on its theology.

views.H: Irrigation channels watered the gardens of Egypt and Mesopotamia and some in Israel (21:1). Flat roofs were living space (21:9). Kings relied on horses and chariots in war, despite the Law's warning (21:31; Deuteronomy 17:16). Sacrifice at the temple was the center of Israel's worship (21:3, 27).
views.C: The Greek lacks 21:5 and has different wording in several verses (21:6, 12, 16, 18). 21:9 is repeated word for word in 25:24, and 21:2 echoes 16:2. The Ketiv and Qere differ at 21:29 and elsewhere. The rare words of 21:8 are debated.
views.W: Egyptian and Mesopotamian kings claimed to rule by the gods' choice and guidance. The image of the gods turning human plans, and the idea that the gods give victory in battle, are common in ancient royal inscriptions.
views.J: The Talmud cites 21:1 to show that a good king is one of three things a person should pray for (Berakhot 55a), reads 21:14's secret gift as charity given in secret (Bava Batra 9b), and reads 21:30 to explain why Phinehas acted without consulting his teacher (Sanhedrin 82a). Rashi reads 21:12's 'Righteous One' as God.
views.X: Augustine cited 21:1 to show that God works in human hearts, even of kings, to accomplish his will (On Grace and Free Will). 21:3 is read with Hosea 6:6 and Jesus' use of it (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), and 21:31 is often quoted with Psalm 20:7.

deep.b:
A number of sayings in Proverbs appear twice, word for word or nearly so. In chapters 16–22 these include 16:25 (= 14:12), 18:8 (= 26:22), 19:1 (≈ 28:6), 19:5 and 19:9, 19:12 and 20:2, 19:24 (≈ 26:15), 19:25 and 21:11, 20:10 and 20:23, 20:16 (= 27:13), 21:9 (= 25:24), 22:3 (= 27:12) and 22:13 (≈ 26:13). Half-lines repeat too, such as 18:11a (= 10:15a) and 18:12b (= 15:33b).

The repetitions show that the book's collections were made from a common stock of sayings, gathered at different times by different editors (25:1). For readers they work like a refrain: a saying met again in a new setting shows a new side. This translation renders repeated Hebrew the same way each time, so that readers can see the repetition.

echoes: Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; Psalm 20:7; 1 Corinthians 1:19–25; Ecclesiastes 9:13–18; Luke 16:19–31; Proverbs 25:24; Proverbs 16:2

settings.what: Sayings on the LORD's rule over kings and plans, justice and sacrifice, home life and wealth
settings.by: the collectors of the Solomon proverbs, framing the chapter with sayings on the LORD's rule (21:1–3, 30–31)
settings.to: young men who would one day offer sacrifice, run households and serve kings
settings.when: under the monarchy, many scholars think, while the temple's sacrifices (21:3, 27) and royal armies (21:31) were part of daily life
settings.why: To teach a young person who would serve kings, offer sacrifice and run a household that God rules over all of these, so that justice matters more than ritual and trust in the LORD more than horses. Knowing these were sayings for future officials explains their frankness about kings and courts.
settings.readers: Readers after the exile, under foreign kings, took 21:1 as comfort: even the kings of Persia were in the LORD's hand (Ezra 1:1; 7:27).
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

title: The Words of the Wise
sum: The first Solomon collection ends at 22:16. Its last sayings speak of a good name worth more than riches (22:1), rich and poor made by the same LORD (22:2), the shrewd man who sees danger coming (22:3), humility and its rewards (22:4), training a young person in his way (22:6), the borrower as the lender's slave (22:7), the generous eye (22:9), driving out the mocker (22:10), the lazy one's lion in the street (22:13), the strange woman's mouth as a deep pit (22:14), folly bound up in a child's heart (22:15), and two roads to poverty (22:16).

At 22:17 a new section begins, 'the words of the wise', running to 24:22. The teacher speaks in the first person, calls for attention (22:17–21), and writes 'thirty sayings' (22:20) to make the pupil a trustworthy messenger. The first sayings forbid robbing the poor (22:22–23), befriending a hothead (22:24–25), standing surety (22:26–27) and moving boundary stones (22:28), and praise the skilled worker who will serve kings (22:29). This opening closely follows the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.
readings: Read as a teacher's charge

The sayings of 22:17–29 are addressed to a 'you' being trained for public service: he will carry answers back to those who send him (22:21) and stand before kings (22:29). Read this way, the passage is a curriculum for young officials, with its moral core in justice for the poor.
Read through 22:6

Many readers take 22:6, 'Train a young person according to his way', as the theme of the whole book: wisdom is formation, begun early and kept for life. The verse's exact sense is debated (see the notes), but its place near the end of the Solomon collection gives it weight.
Read beside Amenemope

Since 1924 readers have compared 22:17–23:11 with the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. The comparison shows Israel's sages using the best wisdom of their neighbors, and setting it under the LORD (22:19, 23).

views.H: The final sayings of the Solomon collection reflect village and court life: debt slavery (22:7), the town square (22:13), boundary stones (22:28), and the young man training for royal service (22:29). The words of the wise (22:17–24:22) seem to come from a school for scribes and officials, like those in Egypt, where pupils copied instructions and learned to carry messages (22:21).
views.C: Critical scholars generally agree that 22:17–24:22 is a separate collection, and that 22:17–23:11 depends in some way on the Instruction of Amenemope, an Egyptian work most date to the Ramesside period (roughly 1300–1075 BC). The emendation 'thirty' at 22:20 is widely accepted; it is the only place in Proverbs 16–22 where the Plain English Translation leaves the Masoretic Text. The Greek lacks 22:6 and adds lines after 22:8, 22:9 and 22:14.
views.W: The Instruction of Amenemope is a teaching by an Egyptian official to his son, in thirty chapters. Its prologue promises to teach a man to answer those who speak to him and carry back a report to the one who sent him; it warns against robbing the poor, befriending a hothead and moving boundary markers, and it ends with the skilled scribe who becomes a courtier. All of these appear in 22:17–29.
views.J: The Talmud reads 22:6 as a debate over the age for training, sixteen to twenty-two or eighteen to twenty-four (Kiddushin 30a), and cites 22:22–23 against corrupt judges (Sanhedrin 7a) and 22:29 in praise of Solomon (Sanhedrin 104b). Rashi reads the 'thirds' of 22:20 as the three parts of the Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings.
views.X: 22:6 is one of the most quoted verses in Christian teaching on parenting, often taken as a promise. 22:15 has been cited in debates on corporal punishment. The Greek addition at 22:8, 'God blesses a cheerful man and a giver', seems to lie behind Paul's 'God loves a cheerful giver' (2 Corinthians 9:7).

deep.h: Proverbs and the Instruction of Amenemope
deep.b:
In 1923 E. A. Wallis Budge published a papyrus in the British Museum containing the Instruction of Amenemope, an Egyptian official's teaching to his son in thirty numbered chapters, and he was the first to note its likeness to Hebrew wisdom; his 1924 translation compares its opening lines with Proverbs 1. In 1924 Adolf Erman showed in detail that Proverbs 22:17–23:11 runs parallel to it. The opening call to listen and store the words 'in the treasure-house of thy belly' matches 22:17–18; the aim of carrying back a report to the one who sent you matches 22:21; Amenemope's warnings against plundering the poor (chapter 2), befriending the hot-headed man (chapter 9) and encroaching on boundaries (chapter 6) match 22:22, 22:24 and 22:28; and his closing chapter, 'Behold the Thirty Chapters!', with its scribe skilled in his profession who becomes equal to the king's friends, matches 22:20 and 22:29. More parallels follow in 23:1–11, on eating with a ruler, wealth that flies away like a bird, and the fields of orphans.

What the parallel shows. Most scholars think the Hebrew sage knew Amenemope, directly or through an intermediate version, and adapted it. Israel's wisdom drew openly on its neighbors' wisdom (1 Kings 4:30–31), and the borrowing was selective. The Hebrew follows its own order, not Amenemope's, shortens and recasts what it takes, and places it under the LORD: 'so that the LORD will be the one you trust' (22:19), 'the LORD will argue their case' (22:23).

What it does not show. The parallels are of thought, image and order of topics, not word-for-word translation. Many of the sayings in 22:17–24:22 have no counterpart in Amenemope, including the warning on surety (22:26–27) and most of 23:12–24:22. The 'thirty' sayings of Proverbs cannot be matched one by one with Amenemope's thirty chapters, and scholars divide the section differently. A few early scholars argued that Amenemope borrowed from the Hebrew; this view has few followers now, but John Ruffle and others have cautioned that the parallels are looser than often claimed and need not mean a written source on the sage's desk. The relationship says nothing against the book's inspiration in the eyes of those who believe it inspired; it shows how Israel's sages worked.

Few verses in Proverbs are better known, and few are more debated. The verb chanakh means to dedicate or start; the noun na'ar covers anyone from a baby to a young man or a squire; and 'according to his way' can mean the right way, the child's own aptitude, or his own willful way. Each reading gives the verse a different force: a call to moral training, to education fitted to the child, or a warning that a child left to himself will stay as he is.

Whatever 'his way' means, the verse is a proverb, not a promise. Proverbs states what usually happens, and the book itself knows of sons who break their parents' hearts (17:21, 25; 19:26). Parents whose children have turned away are not proved faithless by this verse, and children are not freed from responsibility for their own choices (Ezekiel 18:20). The Vulgate seems to sense this when it begins the verse with 'proverbium est', 'it is a proverb'.

echoes: Ephesians 6:4; 2 Corinthians 9:7; Galatians 6:7; Matthew 6:22–23; Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17; Ezra 7:6; Proverbs 23:10–11; Proverbs 27:12; Proverbs 26:13

settings.what: The last sayings of the first Solomon collection: name and riches, rich and poor, training the young, debt, generosity, laziness and the rod
settings.by: the sages who gathered "the proverbs of Solomon" (10:1)
settings.to: young men of Israel's households, and perhaps young scribes and officials in training
settings.when: collected under the kings of Judah, many scholars think, from sayings that may be older
settings.why: To close the collection with sayings on what lasts, a good name, the fear of the LORD, a young person's training, and on the dangers of debt, oppression and laziness. Knowing that these were sayings for the young explains why training (22:6) and discipline (22:15) stand side by side here.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book have often taken 22:6 as a summary of the whole book's purpose: to train the young in wisdom's way (1:4).
views: For the debate over court school, village wisdom and post-exilic editing, see the card at 16:1–9.

settings.what: The opening of 'the words of the wise': a teacher's call to listen, and the first five warnings
settings.by: an unnamed sage who speaks as 'I' (22:17, 19–21), drawing on the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope
settings.to: a young man in training for public service, who will carry messages for those who send him (22:21) and may one day serve kings (22:29)
settings.when: under the monarchy, many scholars think, when Judah's court had contact with Egypt; Amenemope itself is usually dated to roughly 1300–1075 BC
settings.why: To train a future official in the honesty and justice his office demands: to be a truthful messenger, to protect the poor, to avoid hotheads and rash guarantees, to respect old boundaries, and to excel at his work. Knowing that it adapts an Egyptian school text explains its form, a numbered set of instructions addressed to a pupil, and its new center, trust in the LORD (22:19).
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book took 'the words of the wise' as a second voice beside Solomon's, and Jewish and Christian readers before 1924 knew nothing of the Egyptian parallel; Rashi heard in the 'thirds' of 22:20 the three parts of the Hebrew Bible.
views: Most scholars think the sage adapted Amenemope, directly or through an intermediate version, and set its teaching under the LORD.
Some, following cautions like Ruffle's, think both texts drew on a shared international tradition of scribal teaching, and that the links are looser than often claimed.
A few early scholars argued that Amenemope drew on a Semitic original; this view has few followers now.
